title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: NVIDIA no longer sells components; it sells the entire AI factory—from the custom ARM CPU and liquid-cooled GPU rack down to the networking fabric and inference microservices.
epigraph.author: Data Center Systems Architecture

web_blocks.html: NVIDIA reports two GAAP operating segments: Compute & Networking and Graphics [2, 4]. It also tracks four market platforms: Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive [2, 4]. In Q3 FY27, non-Data-Center platforms were grouped under Edge Computing at $8.2 billion [2]. Data Center generated $193.74 billion in FY2026, or 89.7% of the $215.94 billion total [4]. By Q3 FY27, Data Center surged to $107.6 billion, or 92.9% of the $115.8 billion quarterly total [2]. Compute & Networking drives nearly all operating leverage. Gross margins held at 71.1% in FY26 and reached 74.8% in Q3 FY27 [1, 4].

web_blocks.takeaway: Data Center now drives ~93% of NVIDIA's revenue, with ACIE (+195% YoY) growing nearly 3x faster than Hyperscale (+71% YoY) in Q3 FY27, diversifying demand beyond the top four U.S. clouds.

web_blocks.html: 1. Data Center Compute & Networking (92.9% of Q3 FY27 revenue): NVIDIA's flagship product is no longer a PCIe card. It is the Vera Rubin NVL72 liquid-cooled rack-scale supercomputer, which generated nearly $20 billion in Q3 FY27 [6, 12]. One NVL72 rack houses 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 custom Vera ARM CPUs across 18 compute trays [12, 13]. Each Rubin GPU uses TSMC N3 silicon with 288 GB of HBM4 memory [12]. Nine NVLink 6 switch trays link the rack, delivering 260 TB/s of aggregate scale-up bandwidth [12, 13]. Networking alone surpassed $21 billion in Q3 FY27 [2]. Key networking products include ConnectX-9 SuperNICs, BlueField-4 DPUs, Quantum-X800 InfiniBand, and Spectrum-6 Ethernet [2, 12]. Concrete End-to-End Example: A frontier AI lab or neocloud like CoreWeave orders a 10,000-GPU Vera Rubin cluster. NVIDIA designs the rack topology and supplies the GPUs, CPUs, NVLink switches, and Spectrum-X Ethernet fabric [12]. It also bundles NVIDIA AI Enterprise / NIM microservices at $2,000–$4,500 per GPU annually [17]. Customers can deploy multi-agent inference workflows immediately without rewriting CUDA kernels [12, 17].

2. Gaming & AI PCs (7.4% of FY26 revenue; ~$16.04B): Gaming remains a highly profitable cash-generative franchise [4]. It relies on GeForce RTX discrete GPUs for desktops, laptops, and Nintendo Switch SoCs [4]. In 2026, NVIDIA expanded into local AI PCs via RTX Spark laptops and DLSS 5 neural rendering [2]. Concrete End-to-End Example: A PC gamer or developer buys a GeForce RTX 5090 or 5080 card. Partners like ASUS or MSI build the board using NVIDIA's GPU die and reference design. DLSS 5 uses dedicated Tensor Cores to upscale 1080p frames into 4K at high frame rates. The same card also runs local 14B-parameter coding assistants offline.

3. Professional Visualization (1.5% of FY26 revenue; $3.19B): ProViz supplies workstation GPUs and Omniverse 3D simulation software to architects, filmmakers, and industrial engineers [4]. Concrete End-to-End Example: BMW or Foxconn builds an Omniverse digital twin of an assembly plant before pouring concrete. Engineers simulate robot arm paths and warehouse logistics on dual-GPU RTX workstations. That workflow eliminates costly physical factory retooling.

4. Automotive & Physical AI Robotics (1.1% of FY26 revenue; $2.35B): NVIDIA's Automotive platform spans three computing layers [4]. It pairs cloud DGX clusters for training with Omniverse for synthetic sensor simulation. In-vehicle DRIVE Orin / DRIVE Thor SoCs then run real-time inference [4]. Concrete End-to-End Example: An automaker like Mercedes-Benz or BYD integrates a DRIVE Thor centralized computer into its 2026–2027 vehicles. A single safety-certified chip handles highway navigation, parking, and cockpit AI. That model generates upfront silicon revenue plus ongoing fleet software updates.

web_blocks.title: The ACIE Inflection: Non-Hyperscale Demand Hits $47.5B/Quarter
paragraphs: A key shift in Q3 FY27 was the rise of AI Clouds, Industrial, and Enterprise (ACIE) revenue to $47.5 billion (+195% YoY) [2]. Hyperscale revenue reached $60.1 billion (+71% YoY) in the same period [2]. Sovereign AI buildouts, neoclouds, and industrial enterprises are scaling faster than traditional cloud titans. That diversification partially cushions hyperscaler concentration.

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand what NVIDIA actually sells in late 2026, forget the old mental picture of a teenager snapping a GeForce graphics card into a desktop PC. Yes, Gaming is still a $16 billion-a-year business, and it still prints cash. But today, roughly 93 cents of every dollar walking through NVIDIA's door comes from the Data Center—and the product isn't a single chip. It's a complete, liquid-cooled AI factory.

Let's walk through all four of NVIDIA's market platforms with concrete, end-to-end examples so you can see how the hardware and software lock together. Start with Data Center, which delivered $193.74 billion in FY2026 and $107.6 billion in Q3 FY27 alone. Imagine a sovereign AI consortium or a neocloud operator standing up a frontier reasoning cluster. They don't buy loose GPUs anymore; they buy Vera Rubin NVL72 racks. Each rack packs 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 custom Vera ARM CPUs wired together with NVLink 6 switches so all 72 chips behave like one giant processor with 20.7 terabytes of HBM4 memory.

Around those racks, NVIDIA sells the high-speed plumbing—ConnectX-9 SuperNICs, BlueField-4 DPUs, and Spectrum-6 Ethernet or InfiniBand switches—a networking business that by itself topped $21 billion in Q3 FY27. Then, sitting on top of the hardware, NVIDIA layers NIM microservices and NVIDIA AI Enterprise software, pitched at $2,000 to $4,500 per GPU per year, so enterprise IT teams can deploy AI agents without hiring a PhD compiler team.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Notice how NVIDIA's three smaller segments—Gaming ($16.04B), ProViz ($3.19B), and Automotive ($2.35B)—aren't random side projects. They are feeder ecosystems that train developers on CUDA, fund Omniverse physics simulation, and extend NVIDIA's silicon into physical robotics and autonomous vehicles.

book_subsections.title: Inside the Other Three Platforms: Gaming, ProViz & Automotive
paragraphs: Even though Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive together represent roughly 7% of Q3 FY27 revenue ($8.2 billion under Edge Computing), each one solves a real-world problem at high gross margins. In Gaming, a player buying an ASUS or MSI laptop with a GeForce RTX GPU gets DLSS 5 neural frame generation, turning modest power budgets into smooth 4K visuals while running local AI assistants offline.

In Professional Visualization, an automotive or electronics manufacturer uses RTX workstations and Omniverse to build a 3D digital twin of an entire factory floor, catching assembly-line bottlenecks in software before spending a dollar on physical robots. And in Automotive, an OEM embeds NVIDIA's DRIVE Orin or DRIVE Thor SoC into the car's central computer—after first buying NVIDIA DGX servers to train the driving neural networks in the cloud. That 'three-computer' loop—cloud training, simulation, and edge inference—is how NVIDIA turns a single customer into a multi-year platform buyer.

book_subsections.title: Why Compute & Networking Dominate Operating Leverage
paragraphs: Step back and look at the GAAP segment split in Q3 FY27: Compute & Networking generated $106.0 billion (+108% YoY), while Graphics generated $9.8 billion (+62% YoY). Even inside Graphics, AI features like DLSS 5 and local RTX Spark inference are driving the upgrade cycle, lifting Edge Computing to $8.2 billion (+42% YoY). Yet it is the Data Center platform—$107.6 billion in Q3 FY27, split between $60.1 billion Hyperscale and $47.5 billion ACIE—that gives NVIDIA its 74.8% gross margin and 66% trailing operating margin.

What makes that $107.6 billion figure so remarkable is the attach rate of full-system components. Instead of selling a customer a bare GPU and letting Arista or Broadcom supply the switches and Dell supply the chassis, NVIDIA captures the Vera ARM CPU (88 Olympus cores connected via 1.8 TB/s NVLink-C2C), the NVLink 6 switch trays (260 TB/s rack bandwidth), and the Spectrum-6 Ethernet or Quantum-X800 InfiniBand fabric ($21B+ per quarter). Add NVIDIA AI Enterprise and NIM microservices on top, and every rack becomes a multi-layered revenue engine.
